title: Intents & PendingIntent
scopeHtml: Intent resolution, extras, package visibility, exported components, PendingIntent flags and security, chooser/share, and app-link verification at the intent level.

notes.title: Explicit and implicit intents
notes.html:
What it is. An Intent is a small message that says "I want something done". An explicit intent names the exact component that must receive it (the class). An implicit intent only describes the job ("view this URL", "send this text") and lets the system find who can do it.

// Explicit: goes to exactly this class
startActivity(Intent(this, CheckoutActivity::class.java))

// Implicit: system looks for a matching intent filter
startActivity(Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, Uri.parse("https://example.com/p/42")))

Mechanism. startActivity goes through Binder to ActivityTaskManagerService in system_server, which asks PackageManagerService to resolve the intent. Explicit: the ComponentName is looked up directly. Implicit: the system matches action, category and data against every installed intent filter. If nothing matches, ActivityNotFoundException is thrown. If several match, the user sees a chooser (or the saved default app is used).

Security rules. Since API 21, bindService() with an implicit intent throws IllegalArgumentException, and startService with an implicit intent also fails for apps targeting 21+. Implicit service intents are a hijack risk because any app can declare a matching filter. For mutable PendingIntents, implicit base intents are also restricted on API 34 (see the PendingIntent sections).

Real examples. Swiggy or Zomato opening Google Maps for directions uses an implicit geo: or maps https VIEW intent. Paytm and PhonePe launching UPI apps use implicit upi://pay intents and list whoever can handle them. WhatsApp appearing in the share sheet of Gallery is an implicit ACTION_SEND. Navigation between your own screens is almost always explicit.

Real-life picture. Explicit is posting a letter to "Flat 4B, Rose Apartments". Implicit is pinning a note on the society board: "Need a plumber", and whoever is qualified replies.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an implicit intent to bind or start a service. It throws on modern targets and is a security smell.
  • Not guarding implicit startActivity with try/catch for ActivityNotFoundException; on API 30+ resolveActivity also needs package visibility.
  • Assuming implicit means "slower". The cost is negligible; the risk is security and ambiguity.

notes.title: Intent filters and resolution
notes.html:
What it is. An intent filter is a component's "I can handle these jobs" sign in the manifest. A filter has three tests: action, category, data. An implicit intent must pass all three for a component to match.

<activity android:name=".ProductActivity" android:exported="true">
  <intent-filter>
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW"/>
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/>
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE"/>
    <data android:scheme="https" android:host="shop.example.com" android:pathPrefix="/p/"/>
  </intent-filter>
</activity>

The rules that bite.

  • Action: the intent's action must be in the filter's list. A filter with no actions matches nothing.
  • Category: every category in the intent must be in the filter. startActivity silently adds CATEGORY_DEFAULT, so a filter meant for implicit launching must declare DEFAULT, or it is never found. (MAIN/LAUNCHER is the exception because the launcher uses an explicit component.)
  • Data: matching is on URI scheme, host, port, path and MIME type. If the filter specifies a scheme, the URI must have it. Several <data> elements in one filter are merged into a cross product (scheme x host x path), which surprises people: two <data> lines with different scheme and host in one filter also match the mixed combinations.
  • BROWSABLE is required if a link tapped in a browser should open the app.
  • android:priority only helps ordering in narrow cases; do not rely on it to beat another app.

Resolution outcome. Zero matches: ActivityNotFoundException. One: launched. Many: a disambiguation dialog or the user's saved default (Settings, "Open by default"). For https links with verified App Links, the verified app wins without a dialog.

Real examples. Spotify registering for https://open.spotify.com/track/... is a VIEW + BROWSABLE + DEFAULT filter with a path prefix. Gmail registers for mailto:. Camera apps register for IMAGE_CAPTURE. Many apps declare ACTION_SEND with image/* to appear as share targets.

Real-life picture. A hotel concierge desk with a list: "we handle taxis, tours, laundry". Your request must match the service name (action), the request type slip (category) and the details (data) before the concierge accepts it.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting CATEGORY_DEFAULT so a custom-action filter is never matched by startActivity.
  • Writing one <intent-filter> with many <data> tags and expecting them to be independent. Use separate filters for unrelated hosts/paths.
  • Thinking android:priority lets your app win over another app's filter.
  • Putting autoVerify on a filter that is not http/https.

notes.title: Intent extras and Bundle limits
notes.html:
What it is. Extras are key-value pairs attached to an Intent (stored in a Bundle). They carry the small data a screen needs (an id, a mode flag).

Mechanism. A Bundle is a map that can be written to a Parcel. When an intent crosses a process boundary, the whole thing is flattened to bytes and copied through the Binder transaction buffer. Even an intra-app startActivity goes to system_server and back, so it is parceled. Also onSaveInstanceState bundles are sent to system_server when your Activity stops, so the same limit applies there.

The limit. The Binder transaction buffer is about 1 MB per process, shared by all in-flight transactions (not per call). The safe budget for one intent or saved state is tens of KB, not "just under 1 MB". Exceeding it throws TransactionTooLargeException (logcat shows "!!! FAILED BINDER TRANSACTION !!!"; often wrapped as RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size N bytes).

// Bug: passing a big list through extras
intent.putExtra("photos", ArrayList(hugePhotoList))   // TransactionTooLargeException
// Fix: pass an id, load from Room / a repository / ViewModel
intent.putExtra("albumId", album.id)

What goes wrong in production. The crash often appears in onStop (saved state is sent then), not where you added the data; the stack points to ActivityThread.handleStopActivity or ActivityClientRecord. Crashlytics clusters it on low-end devices with many fragments or large saved state. To measure in debug: Parcel.obtain().also { it.writeBundle(b) }.dataSize().

Rules of thumb. Store ids/URIs, not objects. Keep screen state in a ViewModel plus SavedStateHandle (small ids only). Large data lives in Room, a disk file, or an in-memory repository, and travels as an id or a content:// Uri.

Real examples. Google Photos passes a media id/URI to the viewer, not bitmaps. WhatsApp passes a chat id, then loads messages from SQLite. Instagram passes ids for posts and stories.

Real-life picture. The post office pigeonhole is one small box shared by everyone queuing. Do not try to mail a sofa through it; send the delivery address instead.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the limit is "1 MB per transaction". It is shared across all in-progress transactions of the process.
  • Blaming startActivity when the crash is really onSaveInstanceState at onStop.
  • Putting a Bitmap or list of models in extras.
  • Forgetting that Serializable graphs are bigger than Parcelable ones.

notes.title: Parcelable versus Serializable
notes.html:
What it is. Both turn an object into bytes so it can cross a boundary. Serializable is Java's built-in way (a marker interface, uses reflection). Parcelable is Android's faster way (explicit read/write code, usually generated).

Mechanism. Serializable uses ObjectOutputStream reflection: it writes class metadata, field names and extra bytes, and creates many temporary objects (garbage). Parcelable writes raw fields in order into a Parcel via writeToParcel and reads them via CREATOR.createFromParcel. It is commonly quoted as several times faster and smaller; measure before quoting numbers.

@Parcelize
data class User(val id: Long, val name: String) : Parcelable
// kotlin-parcelize generates writeToParcel + CREATOR at compile time
Parcelable layout:   [id:long][name:len+chars]            (no names, order matters)
Serializable layout: class descriptor + serialVersionUID + field names + values

Gotchas.

  • Parcelable is not for persistence. The format is not versioned or guaranteed stable across OS versions. Never write Parcels to disk or SharedPreferences; use Room, Protobuf or JSON.
  • Read order must match write order exactly, or you get garbage or BadParcelableException.
  • Custom classes in a Bundle need the right ClassLoader when unparceling, otherwise ClassNotFoundException when unmarshalling.
  • API 33 deprecated getParcelable(key) / getSerializable(key) in favour of typed overloads (getParcelable(key, Clazz::class.java), or BundleCompat/IntentCompat), safer against type confusion.
  • @Parcelize requires primary-constructor properties to be parcelable types.

Real examples. Navigation Component Safe Args generates Parcelable-aware argument classes. Retrofit/DTO models are usually not Parcelable; map them to UI models first. AndroidX SavedState is bundle based. Large apps use Parcelize in UI-state classes that must survive process death.

Real-life picture. Serializable is packing a suitcase with a full inventory list stapled to every item. Parcelable is stacking items in a known order because both sides already agreed on the packing list.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Parcelable is fine for disk storage.
  • Changing field order between app versions and restoring old saved state.
  • Believing Serializable is never allowed; it is fine for tiny, rare cases but not hot paths.
  • Forgetting R8 keep rules for hand-written CREATOR fields (default consumer rules usually cover it).

notes.title: Package visibility on API 30
notes.html:
What it is. Since Android 11 (API 30), an app targeting API 30+ cannot see most other installed apps by default. getInstalledPackages(), getPackageInfo("com.other"), queryIntentActivities() return empty or throw NameNotFoundException unless the target is "visible".

Mechanism. PackageManagerService filters results per caller. An app is visible if it is the caller itself, certain system apps, an app the caller already interacts with, one declared in the manifest <queries> element, or the caller holds QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES (Google Play restricts it to a narrow set such as file managers, antivirus, device management).

<queries>
  <package android:name="com.whatsapp"/>           <!-- a specific app -->
  <intent>                                          <!-- anyone who handles this intent -->
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW"/>
    <data android:scheme="https"/>
  </intent>
  <provider android:authorities="com.example.provider"/>
</queries>

Symptom. "Open in WhatsApp" disappears for everyone after bumping targetSdk to 30, because your existence check now returns null. Launching an implicit intent through the system still works; your own lookup is what fails.

Migration under live traffic. Bump targetSdk, list every PackageManager query and resolveActivity call. Prefer <queries><intent> over <package> (more privacy friendly, easier for Play review). Replace "check then start" with try { startActivity(...) } catch (ActivityNotFoundException) { fallback }. Roll out through staged rollout and watch the funnel for "open in app" events. Check libraries: manifest merge adds their <queries>, and some SDKs need extra entries.

Real examples. UPI-capable apps (Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm) need <queries> to list payment apps. AndroidX Browser uses a CustomTabsService query to find a Custom Tabs provider. Mail and dialer helpers need queries for mailto: and tel:.

Real-life picture. A school stops letting students see other classes' registers. You can only look up classmates you have met, or those the office listed for you in advance.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES as a quick fix; Play policy rejects it without a valid use case.
  • Thinking <queries> is needed to launch an implicit intent. It is needed for the lookup.
  • Forgetting the behaviour only applies when targetSdkVersion >= 30.
  • Testing only on devices where the other app was already visible through prior interaction.

notes.title: The exported attribute
notes.html:
What it is. android:exported says whether a component (activity, service, receiver, provider) can be started by other apps. true: yes. false: only your app (same UID) or the system.

Mechanism. The check happens in system_server before delivery: if the target is not exported and the caller's UID differs, you get SecurityException: Permission Denial ... not exported from uid ....

The API 31 rule. If you target Android 12 (API 31)+, every component that has an <intent-filter> must declare android:exported explicitly, or the app fails to install/build (manifest merger error). Before, the default was true when a filter was present, making accidental exposure easy. Content providers default to false when targeting API 17+.

<activity android:name=".MainActivity" android:exported="true">  <!-- launcher: must be true -->
  <intent-filter> MAIN / LAUNCHER </intent-filter>
</activity>
<service android:name=".SyncService" android:exported="false"/>

Why it matters. Every exported component is an entry point for other apps, malware included. Lint, Play pre-launch reports and MobSF flag exported components without a permission. Mitigations: exported=false unless needed; android:permission (signature level for partners); validate every extra; use Binder.getCallingUid() where relevant.

Library trap. A library's manifest merges into yours. Third-party SDK components may be exported. Inspect the merged manifest (Android Studio "Merged Manifest" tab) and override with tools:replace="android:exported" where needed.

Real examples. Deep-link activities in shopping and ride apps (Uber, Airbnb style) are exported by necessity and must validate every parameter. Firebase Messaging internals use permissions to restrict who can reach their receivers.

Real-life picture. Exported is a shop with the front door unlocked to the street. Not exported is a staff room with a keycard.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing exported=false stops PendingIntents you hand out; they run as you and can reach private components.
  • Setting exported=true to "fix" a SecurityException instead of fixing the caller.
  • Forgetting same-UID apps bypass the check.
  • Making the launcher activity non-exported; it must be true on API 31+.

notes.title: PendingIntent identity and flags
notes.html:
What it is. A PendingIntent is a token that lets another app (AlarmManager, NotificationManager, a widget) run an Intent later using your app's identity and permissions. You hand over the right to do one specific thing.

Mechanism. PendingIntent.getActivity/getService/getBroadcast(context, requestCode, intent, flags) asks system_server for a token. The system keeps live PendingIntents keyed by (creator package, type, requestCode, intent per Intent.filterEquals, flags). filterEquals compares action, data, type, package, component and categories, but NOT extras. If a match already exists, you get the same token back.

getActivity(ctx, 0, Intent(A).putExtra("id", 1), 0)
getActivity(ctx, 0, Intent(A).putExtra("id", 2), 0)   // SAME token: id=1 extras may still be used

The classic bug. Two chat notifications use the same requestCode and same intent action; both taps open the first chat because the second call returned the first token and the new extras were ignored. Fixes: unique requestCode (e.g. chat id), unique data (intent.data = Uri.parse("chat://$id")), or FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT to overwrite the extras of the existing token. FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENT invalidates old tokens. FLAG_NO_CREATE only checks existence. FLAG_ONE_SHOT allows a single use.

Mutability flag is mandatory. Since API 31 (targetSdk 31+) you must pass FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE, otherwise IllegalArgumentException: ...Targeting S+ (version 31 and above) requires that one of FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE be specified. The incident: after the targetSdk bump the app crashed at notification creation for every Android 12+ user.

Production patterns. Reminder alarms in a to-do app all open the first task; a stale deep link opens an outdated screen because UPDATE_CURRENT was missing; a FLAG_ONE_SHOT notification stops working after the user taps it once and the process restarts. Debug with adb shell dumpsys activity intents, which lists live PendingIntent records.

Real examples. Chat, ride and calendar apps (WhatsApp, Uber, Google Calendar) create one PendingIntent per entity id for notifications and alarms. Media notifications route play/pause buttons to a MediaSession receiver through PendingIntents.

Real-life picture. A cloakroom ticket: the same ticket number gets you the same coat, however differently you describe it the second time.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing extras are part of PendingIntent identity. They are not.
  • Using requestCode 0 for every notification in a list.
  • Using FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT and forgetting that every holder of that token now sees the change.
  • Omitting the mutability flag when targetSdk >= 31.

notes.title: PendingIntent mutability and hijack
notes.html:
What it is. Mutability decides whether the app that receives your PendingIntent can fill in the blanks of the base Intent before firing it.

Mechanism. FLAG_IMMUTABLE locks the intent: it can only be fired as you built it. FLAG_MUTABLE lets the sender call send(context, code, fillInIntent, ...), which merges fillInIntent into your base intent (it can add missing action, data, extras, and even a component if you left it empty). Historically (targetSdk <= 30) default was mutable, which is the classic vulnerability.

The hijack. If your base Intent is empty or implicit and the PendingIntent is mutable, a malicious app that gets hold of it (for example through a notification listener or an exposed broadcast) can redirect it to its own component or to a private component of yours, running with your permissions.

// Safe default
PendingIntent.getActivity(ctx, id,
    Intent(ctx, DetailActivity::class.java).putExtra("id", id),
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT)

When mutable is genuinely needed. Inline reply (RemoteInput fills the reply text), bubbles, and some system callbacks that add results into the intent (geofencing, activity recognition, location updates delivered by Play Services). For those use FLAG_MUTABLE but set an explicit component on the base intent. On Android 14 (API 34), apps targeting 34+ that create a mutable PendingIntent with an implicit base intent (no component/package) get an exception. Lint has checks for missing or mutable flags.

Defences. Immutable by default; explicit component; unique requestCode; no sensitive data in extras; never hand a mutable PendingIntent to an untrusted receiver.

Real examples. Chat apps with inline reply (WhatsApp, Slack, Gmail) use mutable PendingIntents only for the reply action. Fitness apps (Strava style) use mutable ones for activity-recognition updates.

Real-life picture. An immutable PendingIntent is a sealed envelope: the courier can only deliver it. A mutable one has an empty address line the courier may fill with any address, using your stamp.

Common interview traps.

  • Using FLAG_MUTABLE everywhere "because immutable broke inline reply". Only that one needs it.
  • Believing a signature permission on the receiver stops the hijack; the danger is who holds the token.
  • Forgetting that fillInIntent cannot override a component already set.
  • Not knowing the API 34 rule about implicit base intents.

notes.title: Intent redirection
notes.html:
What it is. Intent redirection (a "confused deputy" bug) happens when your exported component receives an Intent from outside, takes an inner Intent out of its extras, and starts it. The attacker's inner Intent then runs with your app's privileges: it can open your non-exported activities or grant URI permissions.

// VULNERABLE: exported activity
val next = intent.getParcelableExtra<Intent>("next_intent")
startActivity(next)   // attacker aims it at your private PaymentActivity

Why it works. startActivity now comes from your UID, which passes the exported=false check of your private components. A worse variant: the attacker adds FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION plus a URI of your FileProvider/ContentProvider and reads private files. Other sources of the inner intent: results from setResult, a Messenger message, a Service call.

Fixes (following Google's published guidance).

  1. Do not launch intents taken from incoming extras. Use a whitelist or an id-to-screen map.
  2. If you must, sanitize: strip FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION/WRITE/PERSISTABLE, set an explicit component you control, and check the resolved target is what you expect.
  3. Android 13 (API 33) added platform protection: apps targeting 13+ drop intents sent to exported components that do not match a declared intent filter. There is an opt-out removeLaunchSecurityProtection(). Confirm the exact behaviour in the docs.
  4. In debug, StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder().detectUnsafeIntentLaunch() (API 31+) logs unsafe launches.
  5. Play Console can flag "Intent Redirection" findings with a fix deadline.

Audit workflow. Search for getParcelableExtra<Intent> and startActivity(intent.getParcelableExtra(...)), trace data from exported components, add allow-lists, and add a test with a hostile caller app.

Real examples. Many reported cases in Play security bulletins and OEM settings apps follow this shape. A typical one is a login-callback activity that forwards a "continue" intent after authentication.

Real-life picture. A bank clerk who follows any note slid under the glass: "also open the vault". The stranger wrote the note, but the clerk holds the vault key.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking exported=false is enough; the attack walks through your own exported door.
  • Sanitizing the action but leaving URI grant flags.
  • Forgetting setResult, Messenger and Service paths as redirection sources.
  • Assuming only startActivity; sendBroadcast and startService with attacker-chosen intents are the same bug.

notes.title: Chooser and share sheet
notes.html:
What it is. When more than one app can handle an implicit intent, the system shows a chooser. For sharing, Intent.createChooser shows the share sheet. Your app can also be a share target.

val send = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
  type = "text/plain"; putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_TEXT, "Check this out: $url")
}
startActivity(Intent.createChooser(send, "Share via"))

Mechanism. The chooser queries PackageManager for matching filters and ranks them using usage signals and Sharing Shortcuts (Direct Share). To put individual contacts on the top row, publish ShortcutInfoCompat with setLongLived(true) and categories via ShortcutManagerCompat, plus a <share-target> in res/xml/shortcuts.xml. EXTRA_EXCLUDE_COMPONENTS can hide components. Android 14 added custom actions in the sharesheet (confirm API details in docs).

Sharing files. Never share file:// Uris (API 24+ throws FileUriExposedException). Use FileProvider with FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION and ClipData on the intent so the grant applies to whichever target the user picks.

Design trade-off (exported share surface). A share target is an exported activity, so it is attack surface: it receives arbitrary text and streams from any app. Validate MIME types, cap sizes, copy streams in the background with limits, do not trust EXTRA_STREAM Uris (a hostile caller can pass a Uri pointing at your own private provider: confused deputy), and consider a confirmation screen. Keep the number of share targets small (one router activity) and keep it separate from internal screens.

Real examples. WhatsApp, Telegram and Gmail appear as direct-share contacts. Pinterest and Instagram accept shared images as targets. Google Photos shares through FileProvider-style grants.

Real-life picture. A parcel counter at the post office: you drop the box and the counter lists the couriers that can carry it. Direct Share is the counter showing your frequent recipients on the front.

Common interview traps.

  • Sharing with file:// or without URI permission flags (receiver gets SecurityException).
  • Expecting the chooser to appear when only one app matches; createChooser forces it, plain implicit does not.
  • Not setting ClipData, so the grant does not reach the chosen target.
  • Trusting the incoming stream Uri without checking it is not one of your own private files.

notes.title: App Links verification
notes.html:
What it is. App Links are https links that open directly in your app without a chooser, because Android has verified you own the domain.

Mechanism. Add android:autoVerify="true" to a VIEW + BROWSABLE + DEFAULT filter with scheme http(s) and a host. At install time (and periodically) the system fetches https://<host>/.well-known/assetlinks.json and checks that it lists your package name and your signing certificate SHA-256 fingerprint. Response must be HTTP 200 with JSON, reachable publicly, no redirects.

[{ "relation": ["delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls"],
   "target": { "namespace": "android_app", "package_name": "com.example.shop",
               "sha256_cert_fingerprints": ["AA:BB:..."] } }]

Versions. API 23-30: verification result is tracked for the set of hosts, and one failing host could break the link set. API 31+: each domain verified independently via DomainVerificationManager, and the user can approve domains manually in Settings, Open by default. On 12+, unverified web links open in the browser, not a chooser. Play App Signing: use the app signing key fingerprint from Play Console (not just the upload key); debug builds need their own fingerprint entry.

Post-incident pattern. Links suddenly open in the browser: usual causes are a CDN/WAF blocking the verifier, a redirect (www to apex, http to https), wrong content type, a staging cert, a rotated signing key, or a stale cached assetlinks.json. Diagnose with adb shell pm get-app-links com.example.shop, adb shell pm verify-app-links --re-verify com.example.shop, and Google's Digital Asset Links API. Before rotating keys, list both old and new fingerprints in the file. Keep a web fallback page for users whose app is not the default handler.

Real examples. Amazon, Flipkart, Swiggy and YouTube links open straight in the app. Branch and AppsFlyer OneLink host their own assetlinks.json support for deferred deep links.

Real-life picture. A club must prove its member list to the reception desk. Reception phones the club office (your domain) and asks "is this member really yours?" Only if the answer matches can the member skip the queue.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing App Links (verified https, no dialog) with plain deep links (custom scheme or unverified, dialog possible, spoofable).
  • Listing only the upload-key fingerprint when Play App Signing re-signs the app.
  • Serving assetlinks.json behind a redirect, login or geo-block.
  • Assuming verification is instant and visible; it is asynchronous and can fail silently.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Explicit intents name the class; implicit ones are matched by action, category (with automatic DEFAULT) and data against intent filters. Services need explicit intents.
  • Extras travel through the roughly 1 MB shared Binder buffer: pass ids, not data. TransactionTooLarge often fires at onStop from saved state.
  • Parcelable for IPC (fast, not for disk); Serializable only for rare cases; use typed getters on API 33+.
  • API 30 hides other apps: declare <queries>; prefer try/catch around start over pre-checking.
  • android:exported is mandatory with filters on API 31+; every exported component is attack surface.
  • PendingIntent identity ignores extras: use unique requestCode or data. Use IMMUTABLE unless mutable is needed, and then use an explicit component.
  • Intent redirection: never launch an Intent pulled out of an incoming extra; sanitize flags and components.
  • Share targets expand your exported surface; use FileProvider and validate inputs. App Links need a correct assetlinks.json with the right signing fingerprint.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between an explicit and an implicit intent, and when do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you understand the component-addressing model that every other Intent security and visibility question builds on.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An explicit intent names the exact target component (class or package plus class), so the system skips resolution and delivers straight to it. An implicit intent only describes an action and data, and the system matches it against intent filters of installed apps. I use explicit for anything inside my own app, and implicit only when I want any capable app to handle it, such as ACTION_VIEW or ACTION_SEND.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
An Intent is a message object passed to the system server (ActivityTaskManagerService / ActivityManagerService) over Binder. The system decides who receives it.

Explicit: component != null  -> deliver to that component (if exported or same UID / same app)
Implicit: component == null  -> PackageManager resolves against <intent-filter>s
                                0 matches -> ActivityNotFoundException (activities)
                                1 match   -> launch
                                N matches -> chooser / default app
  • Explicit is set via Intent(context, Foo::class.java), setClassName, or setComponent. setPackage() alone makes it implicit but restricted to one app's filters.
  • Services: since API 21, bindService()/startService() with an implicit intent throws IllegalArgumentException ("Service Intent must be explicit"). Always explicit for services.
  • Broadcasts: implicit broadcasts for most manifest-registered receivers are not delivered since API 26 (targetSdk 26+), with a short exemption list.
  • Security: explicit intents cannot be intercepted by another app; implicit ones can be answered by whichever app declares a matching filter.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Explicit: inside my app
startActivity(Intent(this, DetailActivity::class.java).putExtra("id", 42L))

// Implicit: delegate to any browser
val view = Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, Uri.parse("https://example.com"))
try { startActivity(view) } catch (e: ActivityNotFoundException) { /* show fallback */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using an implicit intent for an internal service or internal activity, which lets another app hijack it.
  • Not handling ActivityNotFoundException on implicit launches (no browser, no email client, work profile restrictions).
  • Thinking setPackage makes it explicit. It does not; resolution still runs, just limited to that package.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can you not use an implicit intent for bindService? → Any app could answer the bind and receive your data; since API 21 it throws.
  2. What happens when two apps match? → Chooser shows unless the user set a default, or one is a verified app link.
  3. Can you send an explicit intent to another app's activity? → Only if that activity is exported=true (or permission-protected and you hold it); otherwise SecurityException.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer stops at "specific class vs action". The senior adds the security consequence (interception, redirection), the service/broadcast restrictions by API level, and that explicit does not bypass the target's exported flag.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payments SDK used an implicit intent to its own helper service; a malicious app with a matching filter received the payload on API 19 devices. The fix was setPackage plus an explicit component.

questions.promptHtml: How does the system resolve an implicit intent against intent filters? What are the three tests, and why is CATEGORY_DEFAULT important?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many "my link does not open my app" bugs are filter mistakes. This shows whether you can reason about a manifest instead of copy-pasting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The intent must pass three tests against a filter: action, category, and data (URI and MIME type). Action: the intent's action must be in the filter's list. Category: every category on the intent must be declared in the filter. Data: scheme/host/port/path and MIME type must match. For startActivity the system adds CATEGORY_DEFAULT to the intent, so an activity must declare android.intent.category.DEFAULT to be reachable implicitly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Intent(action=VIEW, data=https://shop.com/item/9, categories={BROWSABLE, DEFAULT})
  filter: <action VIEW/> <category DEFAULT/> <category BROWSABLE/>
          <data scheme=https host=shop.com pathPrefix=/item/>
  action   : VIEW in filter                           -> pass
  category : intent cats subset of filter cats        -> pass
  data     : scheme+host+path prefix match            -> pass
  • Within one <intent-filter> multiple <data> elements are merged into a cross product: scheme=http|https x host=a|b is all four combinations.
  • A filter with no <data> matches only intents with no data and no type. A filter with a scheme but no host ignores host/port/path.
  • Data type only: <data android:mimeType="image/*"/> implies content: and file: schemes by default when no scheme is given.
  • startActivity() implicitly adds CATEGORY_DEFAULT; startActivityForResult and Intent.ACTION_MAIN + LAUNCHER do not need it. Browsers coming from a link need BROWSABLE.
  • Use adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://shop.com/item/9" to test and pm query-activities / dumpsys package to inspect.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity android:name=".ItemActivity" android:exported="true">
  <intent-filter>
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW"/>
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/>
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE"/>
    <data android:scheme="https" android:host="shop.com" android:pathPrefix="/item/"/>
  </intent-filter>
</activity>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting DEFAULT, so the activity resolves from am start with -c but not from startActivity.
  • Mixing app-link filters and custom-scheme filters in one <intent-filter>, creating unintended cross-product combos.
  • Assuming intent filters are a security boundary. They are not; they only route.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does host matching need a scheme in the same filter? → Host/port/path are only evaluated if a scheme is declared.
  2. Is pathPattern a regex? → No, a simplified glob (.*, .), and Android 12 adds pathSuffix/pathAdvancedPattern (API 31).
  3. Can a filter match an intent with a category the filter does not list? → No; intent categories must be a subset of filter categories.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists action/category/data. The senior explains the cross-product rule, the DEFAULT injection, and gives an adb command to prove the resolution rather than guessing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deep-link campaign worked on QA builds and failed on release: the release manifest overlay replaced the filter and dropped BROWSABLE, so email clients opened the web page instead.

questions.promptHtml: How do intent extras work internally, what types can they hold, and what are the size limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Passing big data through Intents causes real crashes (TransactionTooLargeException). This tests knowledge of what is happening behind putExtra.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Extras live in a Bundle (a typed key-value map backed by a Parcel). When the Intent crosses to another process it is parceled and sent through Binder, whose per-process transaction buffer is about 1 MB shared across all in-flight transactions. So extras should be small IDs or tiny values; large payloads go through a repository, file, or content URI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Bundle holds primitives, String, CharSequence, arrays, Parcelable, Serializable, and nested Bundles. Under the hood, values are kept in an ArrayMap until parceled, then in a Parcel.
  • Same-process starts still go through the system server (ActivityTaskManager) via Binder, so the Intent is always parceled. There is no "free" in-process path.
  • Binder transaction buffer: 1 MB total per process (minus overhead), shared by all transactions in flight. Hitting it throws TransactionTooLargeException. On Android 7.0 (API 24) and above, Activity state saving (onSaveInstanceState) crashing this way became a thrown RuntimeException instead of a silent log.
  • Practical safe budget: keep a single Intent plus saved state well under ~100-200 KB. The limit is not a documented per-Intent number, so treat any quoted figure as a guideline.
  • Lazy unparceling: a Bundle is unparceled only on the first read. A bad class in a lazy Parcelable surfaces later as BadParcelableException, often in a different place than the sender.
  • Extras are a trust boundary: any app can send an Intent to your exported component with arbitrary extras of arbitrary types.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Prefer ids
startActivity(Intent(this, OrderActivity::class.java).putExtra(EXTRA_ORDER_ID, orderId))

// Receiver: read defensively, extras can be missing or wrong type
val id = intent.getLongExtra(EXTRA_ORDER_ID, -1L)
if (id == -1L) { finish(); return }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing a list of 500 items or a Bitmap through an Intent.
  • Using unscoped key strings like "id" and colliding with others; define constants with a package prefix.
  • Trusting extras from exported components without validation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the 1 MB limit per Intent? → Per process buffer for all pending Binder transactions, so many small ones can also hit it.
  2. How do you pass a large object between screens? → ID plus repository / ViewModel / file / FileProvider URI.
  3. Why does the crash sometimes show up on the next background, not on startActivity? → The saved instance state Bundle is also parceled to the system server on stop.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Bundle, max about 1 MB". Senior: explains it is shared Binder buffer, that in-process starts also parcel, and designs the screens to pass IDs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed screen passed 300 posts via extras and crashed only on low-end devices when another large transaction was in flight.

questions.promptHtml: Parcelable vs Serializable for passing objects in Intents: why is Parcelable preferred, and how do you implement it in Kotlin safely?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the cost model and the practical gotchas (versioning, persistence, API 33 type-safe getters).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Serializable uses reflection and creates lots of temporary objects, so it is slower and heavier on GC. Parcelable is Android's explicit, reflection-free IPC format, designed for Binder. In Kotlin I use @Parcelize from kotlin-parcelize so I do not hand-write writeToParcel. But Parcelable is not stable storage: never persist it, because the format can change between OS versions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Serializable: Java object graph serialization; reflection to find fields, writes class metadata and serialVersionUID. Output is larger and allocation heavy. It is fine for tiny cases and is cross-platform stable.
  • Parcelable: you write fields in order and read them in the same order via a CREATOR. No reflection, compact, fast. The cost is boilerplate, which @Parcelize removes by generating code at compile time.
  • Parcel is for IPC only. Do not write parcels to disk or the network; the wire format is not guaranteed across versions. Use Protobuf/JSON/Room for persistence.
  • Type-safe reads: getParcelableExtra(String) is deprecated at API 33. Use IntentCompat.getParcelableExtra(intent, key, Foo::class.java) or BundleCompat, which also guard against wrong-type extras from malicious senders.
  • @Parcelize requires the class to be in the same module as the plugin and properties in the primary constructor to be Parcelable-able; non-parcelable fields need @IgnoredOnParcel or a custom Parceler.
  • Binder transfer happens for everything, so smaller is better regardless of choice; a Parcelable that holds a 5 MB list is still a crash.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts: id("kotlin-parcelize")
@Parcelize
data class Product(val id: Long, val name: String, val price: Double) : Parcelable

val p = IntentCompat.getParcelableExtra(intent, "product", Product::class.java)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Persisting Parcel bytes in SharedPreferences or a database.
  • Adding a field and breaking a rolling update of a process that has an old saved state.
  • Parceling objects with references to Context, Views, or a lambda.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does @Parcelize use reflection? → No, it generates writeToParcel and a CREATOR at compile time.
  2. How do you parcel a Map<String, Foo>? → Supported if values are Parcelable/Serializable; otherwise a custom Parceler.
  3. Why is getParcelableExtra(key) deprecated? → It performs an unchecked cast and, with a malicious or buggy sender, throws ClassCastException; the class-aware overload validates the type.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Parcelable is faster". Senior: explains why (no reflection/allocations), the do-not-persist rule, API 33 type-safe getters, and the cost is the Binder size cap either way.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app persisted a Parcel to disk for crash recovery; after an OS upgrade the layout shifted and 2% of users crashed on startup with a Parcel read error.

questions.promptHtml: What is package visibility in Android 11, what does <queries> do, and which APIs does it affect?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A common "worked on Android 10, broken on 11" regression. It also shows whether you understand the privacy model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From Android 11 (API 30), apps targeting API 30+ can only see a filtered list of other installed apps. To see more I declare <queries> in the manifest with specific packages, intent filters, or providers. It affects queryIntentActivities, resolveActivity, getPackageInfo, getInstalledApplications, getLaunchIntentForPackage; they return empty or throw NameNotFoundException for invisible apps. Blindly adding QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES is restricted by Play policy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Automatically visible: your own app, some core system packages, apps that started your app (via startActivityForResult/getCallingPackage), apps you have content provider access to via URI grants or provider authority, and packages that you bind or that bind you in some cases.
  • Declaring visibility:
<queries>
  <package android:name="com.whatsapp"/>
  <intent><action android:name="android.intent.action.SEND"/><data android:mimeType="image/*"/></intent>
  <provider android:authorities="com.example.provider"/>
</queries>
  • Intent-based <queries> is preferred because it is more privacy preserving and handles "any app that can do X".
  • Plain startActivity() with an implicit intent still launches an app even if it is not visible to you; the visibility filter applies to query APIs. The breakage usually arrives in guards: if (intent.resolveActivity(pm) != null) returns null so the button disappears or an error shows.
  • It is based on targetSdk 30+; apps targeting 29 or less see everything on API 30 devices.
  • Library manifests merge their <queries> into yours, so check the merged manifest.
  • QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES needs a Play Console declaration and a core-purpose justification.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES and being rejected at Play review.
  • Testing only on API 29 emulators.
  • Adding <queries> inside <application> (it must be a direct child of <manifest>).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you check if WhatsApp is installed on API 30+? → Declare <package android:name="com.whatsapp"/> under <queries> and use getPackageInfo.
  2. Does startActivity(ACTION_VIEW) need <queries>? → Not to launch, but to pre-check with resolveActivity or queryIntentActivities, yes.
  3. How would you debug? → adb shell dumpsys package <pkg> and the merged manifest viewer, plus Logcat for NameNotFoundException.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "add queries for packages". Senior: prefers intent-based queries, knows launch vs query difference, Play policy on QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES, and library manifest merging.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "Share via X" feature vanished for all Android 11 users after bumping targetSdk to 30 because resolveActivity returned null.

questions.promptHtml: What does android:exported control, and what changed in Android 12 (API 31)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the first security gate for every component, and a classic reason an app fails to install after a targetSdk bump.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: exported says whether components from other apps can start or bind to this component. If targeting API 31+, I must set android:exported explicitly on every activity, service, and receiver that has an <intent-filter>, or the build and install fail. The old default (true when a filter exists) was a footgun, so Android removed the default.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Pre-API 31 default: exported=true if the component has any intent filter, else false. Many apps accidentally exposed internal screens.
  • Android 12 (targetSdk 31+): the manifest merger errors ("Manifest merger failed: android:exported needs to be explicitly specified") and the platform refuses to install if a component with a filter has no value.
  • Explicit components in the same UID/app can always start each other regardless of the flag. The flag only blocks other UIDs.
  • A ContentProvider default exported is false from API 17 on (targeting 17+); providers also use grantUriPermissions and permissions.
  • Launcher activity must be exported=true.
  • Exported components should be treated as public APIs: validate everything, consider android:permission, and prefer signature permissions for inter-app within your own suite.
  • Third-party libraries may add exported components. Check the merged manifest, and use tools:node="remove" or override if needed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<activity android:name=".ShareTargetActivity" android:exported="true">
  <intent-filter> <action android:name="android.intent.action.SEND"/> <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/> <data android:mimeType="text/plain"/> </intent-filter>
</activity>
<service android:name=".SyncService" android:exported="false"/>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting exported=true to "make it work" for an in-app issue; the real cause was a wrong component name.
  • Forgetting that an exported component with a filter is reachable by explicit intents too, so the filter is no protection.
  • Not auditing merged manifests, thereby shipping a library's exported debug activity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does exported=false stop another app from starting it by explicit intent? → Yes, SecurityException unless same UID or system.
  2. Which components are tested by pentesters first? → Exported activities/receivers/providers, then deep link handlers.
  3. Same-UID apps (sharedUserId)? → Can start non-exported components; sharedUserId is deprecated at API 29.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "true means other apps can use it". Senior: treats exported surfaces as an attack surface inventory, audits the merged manifest in CI, and protects with permissions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Upgrading to targetSdk 31 broke the CI build because three SDKs shipped receivers without exported; fixed with manifest tools:replace overrides and an upgraded SDK.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app shows one notification per active order (5-10 per user at peak, about 1.2M DAU). Tapping a notification should open OrderActivity for that order. QA reports that "tapping any notification always opens the first order". The code:

fun notify(ctx: Context, order: Order) {
    val intent = Intent(ctx, OrderActivity::class.java).putExtra("orderId", order.id)
    val pi = PendingIntent.getActivity(ctx, 0, intent, PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
    val n = NotificationCompat.Builder(ctx, "orders")
        .setContentTitle("Order #${order.id}").setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_stat)
        .setContentIntent(pi).setAutoCancel(true).build()
    NotificationManagerCompat.from(ctx).notify(order.id.toInt(), n)
}

Logs show correct notify ids, but OrderActivity.onCreate always receives the first orderId. It reproduces only after two or more orders are posted.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain the mechanics, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Notification ids collide" or "Add FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT". The first is wrong (ids differ), and the second alone is also wrong: it makes the bug appear to move around, with all notifications opening the latest order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it one process? (PendingIntents are cached by the system.) Does it reproduce after app restart? Are these taps going to a running task or cold start? Is launchMode set? Which targetSdk?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident-grade outage but a wrong-screen bug; a hotfix release is warranted. Meanwhile, nothing server-side helps.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) PendingIntent identity collision on requestCode 0 plus equal intents; (b) Activity reuse (singleTop) ignoring new intent in onNewIntent; (c) wrong notification id; (d) stale extras from task re-use.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys activity intents (lists PendingIntentRecords and keys), check that the two records show the same key; read launchMode; log intent.extras in both onCreate and onNewIntent.
  5. Root cause: The system finds an existing PendingIntent through key = (creator package, requestCode, Intent.filterEquals which compares action, data, type, package, component, categories, but NOT extras). All orders use requestCode 0 and the same component, so the second getActivity returns the first PendingIntent with the first extras. Without FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT, extras of the existing one are kept. With UPDATE_CURRENT, extras of all would be overwritten with the latest.
  6. Fix: Make each PendingIntent unique: use a unique requestCode per order, or set a unique data URI.
val intent = Intent(ctx, OrderActivity::class.java)
    .setData(Uri.parse("app://orders/${order.id}"))   // makes filterEquals differ
    .putExtra("orderId", order.id)
val pi = PendingIntent.getActivity(ctx, order.id.toInt(), intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT)

UPDATE_CURRENT is then safe: it refreshes extras for the same order only. 7. Prevention: Lint/code review rule: never use constant requestCode with variable extras; a unit/instrumented test posting two notifications and asserting extras via PendingIntent.getActivity(..., FLAG_NO_CREATE). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cast Long ids to Int blindly for requestCode if ids exceed 2^31; use hashCode or a data URI. I would not use FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENT as it invalidates previously handed-out PendingIntents (a notification the user can still see would stop working).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the tapped activity is singleTop and already on top? → Delivered via onNewIntent; you must call setIntent(intent) and re-read extras.
  • Why not rely on the notification id? → The notification id is a NotificationManager concept, unrelated to PendingIntent identity.
  • How to check if a PendingIntent already exists? → PendingIntent.getActivity(..., FLAG_NO_CREATE or FLAG_IMMUTABLE) returns null if none.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A chat app used requestCode 0 for every message notification. Users reported "always opens the oldest chat". It had survived QA because testers only ever had one conversation active.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames notification ids or adds random flags.
  • Hire: Identifies identity rule (requestCode + filterEquals ignores extras), fixes with unique requestCode.
  • Strong hire: Also explains UPDATE_CURRENT vs CANCEL_CURRENT consequences, onNewIntent, and verifies with dumpsys activity intents.

questions.promptHtml: What is a PendingIntent, and what do FLAG_IMMUTABLE and FLAG_MUTABLE mean? What changed in API 31 and API 34?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: PendingIntent is the most-misused security primitive in Android. The flag rules also cause a very common targetSdk-upgrade crash.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A PendingIntent is a token that lets another process (NotificationManager, AlarmManager, a widget host) run an Intent later, with my app's identity and permissions. FLAG_IMMUTABLE means the receiver cannot fill in or change the Intent's fields; FLAG_MUTABLE allows fillIn. Targeting API 31+, I must specify one of them or it throws. I default to IMMUTABLE and use MUTABLE only when the system must add data, like inline reply. On API 34, a mutable PendingIntent wrapping an implicit Intent (no component/package) throws.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The PendingIntent object is a handle to a record held in the system server (PendingIntentRecord). The sender process can invoke send(), and the Intent runs as the creator app.
  • FLAG_IMMUTABLE has existed since API 23. Since API 31 (targetSdk 31+), creating a PendingIntent without IMMUTABLE or MUTABLE throws IllegalArgumentException.
  • MUTABLE is required when the system must modify the Intent: inline reply (RemoteInput writes results into the Intent's clip data/extras), Bubbles, and PendingIntent used with LocationManager/Activity Recognition callbacks that attach data (use mutable). Anything else should be immutable.
  • Android 14 (targetSdk 34): throws if the PendingIntent is MUTABLE and the base Intent has no explicit component or package set. Escape hatch PendingIntent.FLAG_ALLOW_UNSAFE_IMPLICIT_INTENT exists but I should not use it.
  • Android 12 also restricts notification trampolines: tapping a notification may not start an Activity indirectly via a Service or BroadcastReceiver (targetSdk 31+).
  • Identity flags: UPDATE_CURRENT, CANCEL_CURRENT, NO_CREATE, ONE_SHOT.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val open = PendingIntent.getActivity(ctx, id, intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT)

// Inline reply: system must write RemoteInput results into the Intent
val reply = Intent(ctx, ReplyReceiver::class.java).setPackage(ctx.packageName)
val replyPi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(ctx, id, reply,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using FLAG_MUTABLE "so it works" on everything. That allows other apps to alter unspecified fields.
  • Forgetting setPackage/component on a mutable one, which crashes on targetSdk 34.
  • Library code (older Firebase, WorkManager, ads SDKs) creating PendingIntents without flags; crash at targetSdk 31 until upgraded.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What exactly can a receiver change on a mutable PendingIntent? → Only unset fields via fillIn (e.g. action, data, extras if not already set), when sent with an Intent.
  2. Does IMMUTABLE stop UPDATE_CURRENT from updating extras? → No; the creator replaces the stored Intent; immutability is about the recipient.
  3. Why was the default insecure? → Pre-23 PendingIntents were mutable, and an empty-Intent PendingIntent could be redirected by whoever held it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "needs FLAG_IMMUTABLE since Android 12". Senior: explains the token model, when mutable is genuinely required, the API 34 implicit rule, and the trampolines.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After bumping targetSdk to 31, a crash cluster of IllegalArgumentException: Targeting S+ requires FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE came from a stale analytics SDK, not first-party code.

questions.promptHtml: How can a PendingIntent be abused, and how do you build one safely?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Security-minded seniors treat PendingIntents as delegated authority. This tests threat modeling, not memorized flags.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A PendingIntent runs with my app's identity. If it is mutable and the base Intent is empty or implicit, whoever receives it can fill in the target component and make my app launch or broadcast to something I never intended, including non-exported components or permission-protected ones. So: explicit component, immutable by default, never hand a PendingIntent to untrusted code, and be careful about what I put in extras.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Attacker receives my PendingIntent (e.g. via a notification listener,
a mutable PI placed in a Notification action, or an exported API)
  -> pi.send(ctx, 0, Intent().setComponent(myPrivateReceiver))   // fillIn works if MUTABLE
  -> system executes it AS MY APP -> reaches non-exported component / abuses my permissions
  • Threats: (1) mutable + implicit base Intent lets recipient set component, (2) PendingIntents leaked through exported broadcast extras or Notification content visible to NotificationListenerService (those holders can send them), (3) sensitive extras in the base Intent are visible to the receiver (PendingIntent Intents cannot be read, but results flow back).
  • CVE class: "PendingIntent redirection" reported in many system apps; the 2022 Android 12L/13 hardening and API 34 rule target it.
  • Safe construction: explicit component (Intent(ctx, X::class.java)), FLAG_IMMUTABLE, unique requestCode, minimal extras, setPackage on mutable ones.
  • Sender-side checks when I receive a PendingIntent from others (e.g. a SDK API accepting PI): pi.creatorPackage; avoid sending it with extra Intents I built from untrusted input.
  • Audit: Android Lint UnsafeIntentLaunch, Play Console pre-launch security warnings, and dumpsys activity intents.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bad: empty intent + mutable = recipient picks the destination
PendingIntent.getBroadcast(ctx, 0, Intent(), PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE)

// Good
val i = Intent(ctx, SnoozeReceiver::class.java).setAction(ACTION_SNOOZE)
PendingIntent.getBroadcast(ctx, 0, i, PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking explicit target alone is enough when MUTABLE still lets fillIn set extras/data.
  • Passing PendingIntents inside broadcasts anyone can receive.
  • Believing FLAG_IMMUTABLE protects against leaking: any holder can still trigger it, only not alter it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a PendingIntent leaks but is immutable? → Holder can trigger the exact action; make the target idempotent and validate.
  2. Can you revoke a PendingIntent? → cancel() or recreate with FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENT.
  3. How does the system know who the sender was? → The creator uid is stored in the record; the executed Intent carries my identity, not the caller's.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use IMMUTABLE". Senior: describes the delegation model, concrete leak paths, and designs targets to be safe even when triggered by a hostile holder.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pentest showed a mutable broadcast PendingIntent in a notification could be redirected to a non-exported receiver to trigger "log out all devices".

questions.promptHtml: What is an intent redirection vulnerability? Show how it arises in an exported component and how you prevent it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Google Play flags this specifically. It tests whether you can see a security bug in 10 lines of innocuous code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It occurs when an exported component takes an Intent from an untrusted extra and launches it with my app's identity. The attacker packs a nested Intent aimed at one of my private, non-exported components (or a protected one), and my app starts it for them. Fix: do not launch attacker-supplied Intents; build my own from validated fields, and if I must, check the resolved component is allowed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Attacker app --startActivity(Intent(my.Exported).putExtra("next", Intent(my.PrivateAdmin)))--> Exported
Exported: startActivity(intent.getParcelableExtra("next"))  // runs as my UID
          -> PrivateAdmin starts although exported=false
  • Variants: startService, sendBroadcast, setResult(RESULT_OK, intent) returning an attacker-controlled Intent, flags like FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION inside the nested Intent used to steal content provider access to my private files.
  • Prevention:
    • Prefer parsing simple primitives and mapping to known destinations (when(route)).
    • If forwarding, validate component, then compare against an allowlist and strip dangerous flags (removeFlags(FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION or FLAG_GRANT_WRITE_URI_PERMISSION)).
    • Do not launch if resolveActivity resolves to my own non-exported components.
    • Mark components not exported by default.
  • Tooling: Android Lint check UnsafeIntentLaunch; Android 15 (API 35) added StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder.detectUnsafeIntentLaunch() (verify against the docs for your target); Play Console security warning "Intent Redirection".
  • Related: unsafe getParcelableExtra types can crash the exported component; use the type-checked getters.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Vulnerable
class TrampolineActivity : Activity() {
    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(b)
        val next = IntentCompat.getParcelableExtra(intent, "next", Intent::class.java)
        startActivity(next)            // attacker-controlled target + flags
    }
}

// Safer: map a route to a known destination
val target = when (intent.getStringExtra("route")) {
    "orders" -> OrdersActivity::class.java
    else -> HomeActivity::class.java
}
startActivity(Intent(this, target))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forwarding after only checking the action string.
  • Assuming "internal-only" because the component is hard to guess.
  • Missing the setResult variant and URI grant flags.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does this relate to login flows (OAuth redirect trampolines)? → Common sources; validate redirect Intents to known packages.
  2. Is exported=false enough? → Mostly for entry points; the vulnerable component must be exported or reachable by an attacker-chosen Intent.
  3. How would you test? → Write an attacker APK or use adb shell am start -n ... --eu/drozer, and enable lint.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "validate input". Senior: describes the confused-deputy pattern, URI grant variant, safe mapping approach, and CI lint + Play warnings.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A WebView bridge activity forwarded a next Intent; a researcher used it to open an internal "debug dump" activity and exfiltrate tokens.

questions.promptHtml: How do you implement sharing correctly with ACTION_SEND and the system chooser? How do you share a file securely, and how does your app appear as a share target?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Sharing is in nearly every app; mistakes include permission leaks, crashes, and missing share targets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I build an ACTION_SEND Intent with a MIME type and EXTRA_TEXT or EXTRA_STREAM, wrap it in Intent.createChooser (or ShareCompat.IntentBuilder), and start it. For files I never use file:// URIs; I use a FileProvider content URI with FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION and ClipData. To receive shares, I declare an exported activity with an ACTION_SEND filter and publish sharing shortcuts for Direct Share.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The chooser is a system UI (ChooserActivity) that shows apps whose filters match the Intent. The Intent is evaluated once; extras are visible to the chosen app.
  • file:// URIs throw FileUriExposedException for targetSdk 24+. Use FileProvider.getUriForFile and grant URI permissions. For the chooser, grant must be carried in ClipData + flag on the chooser Intent (the system propagates to the chosen target since Android 5).
  • Direct Share: publish sharing shortcuts (ShortcutManagerCompat.pushDynamicShortcut with a category matching <share-target> in shortcuts.xml). ChooserTargetService is deprecated at API 30.
  • Android 10+ adds Intent.EXTRA_TITLE, preview text/thumbnail on the chooser; Android 14 supports custom chooser actions via EXTRA_CHOOSER_CUSTOM_ACTIONS.
  • Receiving: handle intent.type, treat EXTRA_STREAM as untrusted, read through ContentResolver with a size cap and off the main thread.
  • Chooser always shows (no default), unlike a plain implicit ACTION_SEND where the user may set a default.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(ctx, "${ctx.packageName}.files", file)
val send = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
    type = "image/png"
    putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_STREAM, uri)
    clipData = ClipData.newRawUri("", uri)
    addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)
}
startActivity(Intent.createChooser(send, "Share via"))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using file:// or raw external storage paths.
  • Not setting ClipData, so the grant is not propagated to the target.
  • Sharing sensitive extras (tokens) in EXTRA_TEXT.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How long does the URI permission last? → Until the receiving task/process dies or the device reboots, unless persisted.
  2. How would you share from a non-FileProvider ContentProvider? → Grant via grantUriPermission or flags on the Intent with grantUriPermissions=true.
  3. How do you know which app the user chose? → IntentSender callback via createChooser(intent, title, pendingIntent.intentSender) (API 22+), which requires a mutable PendingIntent with explicit component.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: createChooser + EXTRA_TEXT. Senior: FileProvider/ClipData grants, Direct Share shortcuts, handling the receiving side securely.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Sharing images crashed on a Samsung Android 9 device: file:// URI with targetSdk 28 led to FileUriExposedException.

questions.promptHtml: At the intent level, how does an HTTPS link open your app directly without a disambiguation dialog? How does verification work, and why does it fail?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Deep links are central to growth features; the verification flow changed in Android 12 and still fails silently. (Jetpack Navigation deep links are covered in A4.)

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I declare an intent filter with autoVerify="true", ACTION_VIEW, DEFAULT, BROWSABLE, and http/https scheme with the host. The system downloads https://host/.well-known/assetlinks.json, and checks that it lists my package name and signing certificate SHA-256. If verified, links to that host open my app directly. Otherwise the user sees a chooser (Android 6-11) or the link opens in the browser (Android 12+).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Install/update  -> PackageManager triggers verification (Android 12+: domain verification agent)
                -> GET https://shop.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json  (no redirects)
                -> match package + sha256_cert_fingerprints + relation delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls
Result stored per domain per package; user can override in Settings > Open by default
  • Android 6-11: verification at install; for each host in autoVerify filters, if one host fails, the whole app's autoVerify for all hosts may be treated as failed on older releases.
  • Android 12 (API 31): verified per domain; unverified web intents no longer show app in the disambiguation chooser; they go to the default browser. Non-verified apps can be approved manually by the user ("Open supported links").
  • Android 15 and Play Console adds Deep link validation tooling; adb shell pm get-app-links <pkg> shows state; adb shell pm verify-app-links --re-verify <pkg> retriggers; pm set-app-links can force for testing on a debug device.
  • Failure causes: wrong fingerprint (Play App Signing key differs from upload key), redirect from apex to www, file served with wrong content type or behind auth/geo block, an unreachable host during install, filter mixing custom scheme in the same filter with autoVerify.
  • Intent-level: you should still handle the incoming URI as untrusted input (intent.data) and validate path/params before routing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
  <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW"/>
  <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/>
  <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE"/>
  <data android:scheme="https" android:host="shop.com"/>
</intent-filter>
[{"relation":["delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls"],
  "target":{"namespace":"android_app","package_name":"com.example.shop",
            "sha256_cert_fingerprints":["AA:BB:..."]}}]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the upload key fingerprint instead of the Play App Signing key.
  • A 301 redirect on assetlinks.json (not followed).
  • Testing only on debug builds with different signing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why use a custom scheme in addition? → Works for app-to-app and fallback, but it is not verified and can be claimed by any app.
  2. How do you handle users who disabled link handling? → Cannot force; deep link to Settings ACTION_APP_OPEN_BY_DEFAULT_SETTINGS (API 31).
  3. How to debug a single device? → pm get-app-links, dumpsys package domain-preferred-apps, check host fetch logs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "add autoVerify and assetlinks". Senior: knows the Android 12 change in behaviour, the Play-signing fingerprint trap, no-redirect rule, and the debug commands.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An email campaign link opened the browser for 100% of new installs; the assetlinks listed only the upload key while Play re-signed the app.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 6.12 of a ride-hailing app (9M MAU, 94% on Android 10-14) raises targetSdk 33 to 34. Within an hour Crashlytics shows a new top crash at 1.9% of sessions, almost entirely during ride start:

java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: android.app.PendingIntent: com.example.rides: Targeting U+ (version 34 and above) disallows creating or retrieving a PendingIntent with FLAG_MUTABLE, an implicit Intent within and without FLAG_NO_CREATE and FLAG_ALLOW_UNSAFE_IMPLICIT_INTENT for security reasons.
  at android.app.PendingIntent.checkFlags(PendingIntent.java)
  at com.example.rides.tracking.NotificationFactory.buildReply(NotificationFactory.kt:88)

Staged rollout is at 20%. Crash-free rate dropped from 99.6% to 98.4%. Another smaller crash shows SecurityException: Starting FGS ..., which began in the same release.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix, and how you decide what to do about the second crash.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add FLAG_ALLOW_UNSAFE_IMPLICIT_INTENT" (disables the protection) or "switch to IMMUTABLE" (breaks inline reply), and treating both crashes as the same bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the rollout halting-capable? Does the crash appear only on API 34 devices? Is line 88 first-party? Did anything else change (FGS types)? What is the notification feature (reply, snooze)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout at 20%; consider a server-side kill switch for the feature if one exists; prepare a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) mutable PendingIntent for inline reply with an Intent lacking component/package (stack names it exactly); (b) same pattern in a library; (c) the FGS crash is separate, from API 34 foreground service type requirement; (d) red herring: older devices show no crash.
  4. How I'd verify each: Filter Crashlytics by OS version (all API 34); open NotificationFactory.kt:88; grep FLAG_MUTABLE across modules and dependencies' merged code; reproduce on an API 34 emulator; for the FGS crash read the message: missing android:foregroundServiceType in manifest or missing permission FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION.
  5. Root cause: Reply action built Intent(ACTION_REPLY) with no setPackage/component but needs MUTABLE for RemoteInput. API 34 bars mutable + implicit. The FGS issue is a separate Android 14 requirement: every foreground service must declare a type and matching permission.
  6. Fix: Make the Intent explicit (this fixes it without removing mutability):
val reply = Intent(ctx, ReplyReceiver::class.java).setAction(ACTION_REPLY)
val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(ctx, 0, reply,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT)

Add android:foregroundServiceType="location" plus FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION; hotfix in 6.12.1. 7. Prevention: Test matrix includes the latest API level and targetSdk bump checklist (behavior changes page). Lint is enabled with error level for PendingIntent flags. Crashlytics alert on new fatal issue in staged rollout. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use FLAG_ALLOW_UNSAFE_IMPLICIT_INTENT or roll back targetSdk (Play enforces annual targets); I would not fix both bugs in one blind change without separate verification.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is the bug device-dependent? → It depends on targetSdk 34 and OS 34+; on API 33 devices running the same build, there is no throw.
  • Could you ship a server flag to avoid the crash? → Only if the crash path is feature gated; otherwise a code fix is needed.
  • Why not just target 33 again? → Play requires newer targets; you would be postponing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's targetSdk bump passed QA because all test devices were on API 33; the first API 34 users were internal dogfooders on the hotfix day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suppresses with the unsafe flag or immutability without understanding.
  • Hire: Reads the message, makes the Intent explicit, separates the FGS issue.
  • Strong hire: Halts rollout, explains why explicit is the real fix, and adds process controls (API-level device matrix, behaviour-change checklist).

questions.contextHtml:
A photo-editor app (1.1M DAU) passes selected media between screens. Crash reports: 0.9% of sessions on low-RAM devices (2-3 GB) after the user selects around 150 photos and switches to another app and back.

java.lang.RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1048252 bytes
  at android.app.servertransaction.TransactionExecutor.execute
Caused by: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException

Code:

class GalleryActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private var selected = ArrayList<MediaItem>()      // MediaItem: Parcelable, ~6 KB each (thumb bytes inside)
    override fun onSaveInstanceState(out: Bundle) {
        super.onSaveInstanceState(out)
        out.putParcelableArrayList("sel", selected)
    }
    fun openEditor() = startActivity(Intent(this, EditorActivity::class.java)
        .putParcelableArrayListExtra("items", selected))
}

The adb test with 20 photos never crashes. Another team suspects a Fragment leak (red herring).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure and propose a fix that survives process death.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compress the thumbnails" or "wrap in try/catch". The first lowers the number but keeps the design wrong; the second cannot catch a crash in system-driven state saving.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where exactly is the exception thrown (stop-time state save vs startActivity)? Is the crash reproducible by count? Are items needed after process death? Is there an existing repository/DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap selection or strip the thumb byte arrays from the Parcelable; ship a hotfix reducing payload under ~100 KB.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) saved state too large; (b) extras Intent too large; (c) combined pending transactions on stop; (d) leak/GC (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: 150 x 6 KB = 900 KB, close to the 1 MB shared buffer, plus the Fragment state and view state, so about 1,048,252 bytes matches. Reproduce with adb shell am start flows and a synthetic 150-item selection; log Parcel.dataSize() of the Bundle in debug builds; the stack goes through TransactionExecutor (state save at stop).
  5. Root cause: Bundle parceling for onSaveInstanceState and Intent extras go over Binder; 1 MB buffer shared per process. Math: 150 x 6 KB = ~900 KB plus other state exceeds budget on a heavy screen; 20 photos = 120 KB passes, which is why test did not catch it.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: pass only IDs (LongArray) and drop thumbnail bytes from Parcelable.
    • Long term: store the selection in a Room table or SavedStateHandle with IDs only, resolve to items via repository.
class GalleryVm(private val state: SavedStateHandle, private val repo: MediaRepo) : ViewModel() {
    val selectedIds: StateFlow<List<Long>> = state.getStateFlow("sel", emptyList())
    fun toggle(id: Long) { state["sel"] = (selectedIds.value + id).distinct() }
}
  1. Prevention: StrictMode-style debug check: assert bundle dataSize under 200 KB in a base Activity (Parcel.obtain().use), a lint/review rule against Parcelable lists in extras, a stress test with 500 items on a low-RAM emulator.
